title: Type and reliability of information about coronavirus most frequently shared by social media users
screen_reason: Content analysis of the 120 most-shared COVID-19 articles on Facebook (BuzzSumo, 21 July - 31 August 2020). Each article was subjected to 'a narrow and dichotomous analysis of accuracy to determine whether something was or was not misinformation', and the authors report that none of the 120 qualified ('No myths or misinformation were found in the most frequently shared articles'; 'there were in fact no myths or misinformation in the top 20 every week'). That is a quantitative share of items judged against an accuracy criterion with an explicit denominator (0/120 = 0%), i.e. a CONTENT prevalence estimate of zero. Borderline because the numerator is stated in words rather than as a number/percentage.

estimates.platform: Facebook (content identified via BuzzSumo across Facebook, Twitter, Reddit, Pinterest; analysis limited to Facebook)
estimates.date: 21 July 2020 to 31 August 2020 (six weekly search sessions)
estimates.measure_type: % of the 120 most-shared COVID-19 articles on Facebook classified as myths or misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 0 of 120 articles ('no myths or misinformation were found'; the 120 articles were shared 6,189,187 times)
estimates.denominator: 120 most-shared COVID-19 articles on Facebook (top 10 by total engagement for each of two keywords, in each of six weekly sessions), shared 6,189,187 times in total
estimates.definition: An article counted for the numerator if the authors' dichotomous accuracy judgement classified it as a myth or misinformation; none did, and the pre-planned 'myths and misinformation' category was replaced by 'debunking myths and misinformation'
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition given; operationalised as 'a narrow and dichotomous analysis of accuracy to determine whether something was or was not misinformation'
estimates.source_quote: Among 120 articles that were shared 6,189,187 times in total during the analyzed period, the most popular were those that referred to methods for decreasing COVID-19 spread and characteristics. No myths or misinformation were found in the most frequently shared articles. The most popular content included humorous yet educational videos.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (Results); the same finding is restated in the Results section, p. 2: 'The study covered 120 articles analyzed in detail that were shared 6189,187 times' and 'there were in fact no myths or misinformation in the top 20 every week but rather their explanations only'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Authors (a five-person clinical/public-health team) judged each article's accuracy dichotomously; topic categories were 'predetermined by the means of discussion among authors' and informed by prior published work; no external fact-check source, no coder-agreement statistic reported
estimates.moderator_quote: The search terms were “coronavirus” and “COVID-19′′. ... The articles were selected on the basis of the total engagement parameter in BuzzSumo, which is a sum of reactions, comments and shares in all social media analyzed in this tool. The top 10 articles for each keyword were included in the analysis. Because Facebook was the most engaging platform for users (95% of an entire engagement), we decided to limit the analysis to articles shared on Facebook. ... The categorization of articles involved a narrow and dichotomous analysis of accuracy to determine whether something was or was not misinformation.
estimates.notes: Zero-prevalence estimate. The paper never prints '0%'; the numerator is asserted in words twice (abstract and Results) and the denominator (120 articles) is verbatim, so the share is an exact part/whole from verbatim statements rather than a computed complement. Selection is heavily curated (only the most-engaged articles, English only, free access from the EU), so this is prevalence among top-shared COVID content, not among COVID content generally. Table 2's 3.1% is the share of SHARES going to the 'debunking myths and misinformation' topic - debunking content, not misinformation - and is not extracted.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) The Introduction cites the authors' own earlier study: 'found information on social media about COVID-19 to be usually accurate (80% of all) but account for less shares (64%)' - a figure the paper takes from elsewhere (ref [12]), so not extracted per R8. 2) Table 2 reports the distribution of 6,189,187 shares across eight TOPIC categories (e.g. 'debunking myths and misinformation' 459,300 shares, 3.1%; 11 articles). These are topic shares, not misinformation shares - the debunking category is corrective content - so no SHARING row was created. 3) The Discussion cites a WHO/University of Melbourne survey (49.3% of 23,000 respondents most likely to share scientific COVID content); cited from elsewhere and not an exposure/sharing-of-misinformation share.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. Frame: BuzzSumo searches for 'coronavirus' and 'COVID-19' run weekly over the preceding seven days, 21 July - 31 August 2020 (12 sessions, 6 per keyword); the top 10 articles per keyword per session by total engagement were retained, limited to Facebook (95% of engagement); items excluded if paywalled, unavailable in the EU, without English transcription, or expired. N = 120 articles, 6,189,187 shares. Coding: authors assigned each article to one or more of eight topic categories developed by discussion, plus a dichotomous accuracy (misinformation / not) judgement. No response-rate concept; no inter-coder reliability statistic, no coder count, and no external ground-truth source reported. Authors note comments were not analysed and six weeks may be unrepresentative.
